title: Genesis 11:10–32
context: After Babel, the camera quiets on Shem. Ordinary years carry the promise-line through Arpachshad, Shelah, Eber, Peleg, Reu, Serug, and Nahor to Terah. Abram, Nahor, and Haran are named; Haran dies in Ur; Sarai is barren. Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai toward Canaan, settles in Haran, and dies there—the setup for chapter 12.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: What older interpreters in each camp said about Shem’s line from Arpachshad to Terah and Abram.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: How little do we know of those that are gone before us in this world, even those that lived in the same places where we live! Or indeed of those who are our contemporaries, but in distant places. That there was an observable gradual decrease in the years of their lives.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the Old Testament (on Gen 11:10)

reformed.quote: Concerning the progeny of Shem, Moses had said something in the former chapter Genesis 10:1 : but now he combines with the names of the men, the term of their several lives, that we might not be ignorant of the age of the world. For unless this brief description had been preserved, men at this day would not have known how much time intervened between the deluge and the day in which God made his covenant with Abraham.

verses.text: This is the history of the generations of Shem: Shem was one hundred years old when he became the father of Arpachshad two years after the flood.
verses.arminianNotes:
After Babel’s noise, the camera quiets on Shem. A hundred years old, two years after the flood, he fathers Arpachshad. The promise-line is a date and a birth.

Arminians receive this as ordinary grace: a family kept through judgment so blessing can still reach the nations. The story is not only empires and towers; it is a named son in a named year.
verses.reformedNotes:
Generations of Shem restart the spine that will run to Abram. God timestamps the line two years after the flood.

Calvin noted that Scripture reckons the world’s years from this family as a mark of election’s honor, not the clan’s moral superiority. Providence keeps a thread when the nations scatter.

verses.text: Shem lived five hundred years after he became the father of Arpachshad, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shem lives five hundred years after Arpachshad and has other sons and daughters. The named heir is not the only child.

Long years and unnamed siblings are still gift. God loves more than the spotlight name; fruitfulness around the promise-line is family, not leftover.
verses.reformedNotes:
Five centuries of further life mean Shem outlasts many grandsons. Other sons and daughters fill the house while the recorded line stays thin.

God can keep a promise through one named son without pretending the others do not exist. Ordinary years are the medium of His keeping.

verses.text: Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and became the father of Shelah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Arpachshad fathers Shelah at thirty-five, and the genealogy moves on. The links are short and unadorned.

Classical Arminians see responsible begetting: a man lives, a son is born. The road toward Abram is walked in ordinary decades, not in constant miracle-language.
verses.reformedNotes:
Arpachshad fathers Shelah at thirty-five. The genealogy does not pause to explain.

God is counting. Each fathered son is another kept stitch in the fabric that will reach Terah and Abram.

verses.text: Arpachshad lived four hundred three years after he became the father of Shelah, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Life around the line is long and full.

Unnamed children still receive years. The promise-line does not empty the rest of the household of dignity.
verses.reformedNotes:
The refrain returns: long life, other sons and daughters. God records duration as well as descent.

Providence is not only the next name; it is centuries in which that name’s family simply lives.

verses.text: Shelah lived thirty years, and became the father of Eber.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shelah at thirty fathers Eber—the name that will mark the Hebrews.

An ordinary age, a weighty son. God can hang a people’s later name on a quiet birth.
verses.reformedNotes:
Eber, whose name may lie behind the word “Hebrew,” enters the line here. The line that will be called Hebrew is still just a boy in a list.

Election’s thread is being drawn through Shelah’s house. The significance is God’s, not yet the child’s fame.

verses.text: Shelah lived four hundred three years after he became the father of Eber, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Again the long after-years and other children. Shelah’s story is mostly time.

Classical Arminians let the repetition preach: faithfulness looks like decades of unnamed life around a named son.
verses.reformedNotes:
Four hundred three years after Eber. The clock is the theology.

God is not bored by duration. The promise survives in ordinary years as surely as in the later call.

verses.text: Eber lived thirty-four years, and became the father of Peleg.
verses.arminianNotes:
Chapter 10 already tied Peleg to the earth’s division.

The Babel scatter and this birth belong to the same world. A man names a son in the days the earth is divided; human history and God’s spreading purpose meet in a family.
verses.reformedNotes:
Peleg’s name still carries the division of the earth. The genealogy will not let Babel float free of Shem’s house.

God timestamps nations and a son together. The line continues through the very era He used to fill the world.

verses.text: Eber lived four hundred thirty years after he became the father of Peleg, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eber lives four hundred thirty years after Peleg—the longest of these post-flood lives in the list.

Long life here is gift. The ancestor of the Hebrews is given time, other children, and a place in the story. Ordinary years remain the way God keeps a people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Eber’s after-years are the longest among these names. God is free to portion life as He will.

The Hebrew name’s source is kept through centuries. The line does not run on human vitality alone; the Lord assigns the years.

verses.text: Peleg lived thirty years, and became the father of Reu.
verses.arminianNotes:
Peleg at thirty fathers Reu. Lives are already shortening beside Shem’s centuries.

Ordinary years still suffice to carry a son. The promise does not need antediluvian lifespans to stay alive.
verses.reformedNotes:
The pace of the list is becoming more like later history.

God shortens the years and still keeps the thread. The mandate and the line both proceed on His clock.

verses.text: Peleg lived two hundred nine years after he became the father of Reu, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two hundred nine years after Reu—Peleg’s remaining life is shorter than his fathers’.

Arminians hear mortality settling toward the world Abram will know. Gift remains: sons, daughters, and enough years to hand the line on.
verses.reformedNotes:
Peleg’s after-span is markedly less. The narrator does not moralize; he numbers.

Providence governs even the shrinking of years. The promise-line is not threatened by a shorter life.

verses.text: Reu lived thirty-two years, and became the father of Serug.
verses.arminianNotes:
Reu fathers Serug at thirty-two. Another quiet link.

Most of God’s work toward Abram looks like this—a name, an age, a son. Do not despise the uneventful.
verses.reformedNotes:
Serug is born. The chain is now deep into the post-flood world.

Unnamed decades are still decreed time. God is moving the story by births more than by speeches.

verses.text: Reu lived two hundred seven years after he became the father of Serug, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
The refrain is almost a lullaby—and still true.

Fruitfulness around the line continues. God is kind in the repetitive gifts.
verses.reformedNotes:
The formula holds. Reu’s house is larger than the one name we track.

God’s bookkeeping includes the other children. Election of a line is not contempt for the rest of the family.

verses.text: Serug lived thirty years, and became the father of Nahor.
verses.arminianNotes:
Serug at thirty fathers Nahor—Abram’s grandfather is now in view, still two generations out.

Arminian readers feel the story leaning forward. Ordinary begetting is how God sets the stage for a call not yet spoken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Nahor appears. The names begin to sound like the household of chapter 12.

Providence is already naming the grandfather of the man God will call. The future promise is being prepared in a quiet list.

verses.text: Serug lived two hundred years after he became the father of Nahor, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
Two hundred years after Nahor. Round numbers, other children, no anecdote.

In practice: two centuries of unnamed life still sit inside God’s care. The line does not have to be famous yet to be kept.
verses.reformedNotes:
Serug’s two hundred years close another generation. God needs no extra plot.

The promise-line advances by duration. What looks uneventful is still His keeping.

verses.text: Nahor lived twenty-nine years, and became the father of Terah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ages keep dropping; the next name is Abram’s father.

We are nearly at the household that will leave Ur. Ordinary years have carried us from Shem’s ark-memory to Terah’s door.
verses.reformedNotes:
Terah is born when Nahor is twenty-nine. The genealogy’s aim is coming into focus.

God has been aiming this list. Terah exists because the Lord intended a father for Abram.

verses.text: Nahor lived one hundred nineteen years after he became the father of Terah, and became the father of more sons and daughters.
verses.arminianNotes:
One hundred nineteen years after Terah—the shortest remaining span yet. Nahor’s generation feels nearer to later limits.

Arminians take the shortening as wise disposal, not a narrative accident. The stage for Abram is a world of shorter lives and nearer graves.
verses.reformedNotes:
Nahor’s after-years are brief beside Shem’s. The narrator still adds other sons and daughters.

God portions life. A shorter patriarch does not weaken the oath that will be spoken over his grandson.

verses.text: Terah lived seventy years, and became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran.
verses.arminianNotes:
Seventy years, then three sons: Abram, Nahor, and Haran. The name the next chapter will call is listed with his brothers. Privilege sits inside an actual family.

Classical Arminians linger on Abram named among others. God’s coming call is sincere and particular, yet it does not erase Nahor and Haran. The promise-line is a man who will have to go; his brothers remain part of the story of ordinary kinship.
verses.reformedNotes:
Moses places Abram first, not necessarily as firstborn, but as the son toward whom the book is driving. Three names, one calling soon to fall.

God has been narrowing from Shem to Terah to this trio. Election of Abram will not be a random draw; it is the point this genealogy has been serving. The brothers are not imaginary; the choice is God’s.
verses.keyContrast: Both honor Abram named among brothers. Arminians typically read a particular call that will still address a responsible man inside a family; Reformed commentators often read the genealogy’s narrowing as God’s sovereign preparation of the man He will call.

verses.text: Now this is the history of the generations of Terah. Terah became the father of Abram, Nahor, and Haran. Haran became the father of Lot.
verses.arminianNotes:
A new generations formula: Terah’s house. Haran fathers Lot, who will travel in the next chapters.

In practice: the promise household already includes a nephew. God’s setup for chapter 12 is a family, not a solitary hero.
verses.reformedNotes:
Terah’s generations begin. Lot is named before the journey, because providence already sees the companion—and the later strife.

The camera has left the long list of years and opened a household. God is arranging the cast for the call.

verses.text: Haran died in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Chaldees, while his father Terah was still alive.
verses.arminianNotes:
Haran dies before his father’s face, in Ur of the Chaldeans. Grief sits in the genealogy. The land of kindred is also a place of graves.

Classical Arminians refuse to skip the death. Ordinary years include loss. Ur is already costly before anyone leaves it; the later call will not be tourism.
verses.reformedNotes:
Haran dies in Terah’s presence, in Ur. The promise-line is not spared family funerals.

God records the place—Ur of the Chaldeans—because this is the soil from which He will shortly call. Death in the father’s sight is part of the setup, not an interruption God failed to notice.

verses.text: Abram and Nahor married wives. The name of Abram’s wife was Sarai, and the name of Nahor’s wife was Milcah, the daughter of Haran, who was also the father of Iscah.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abram and Nahor take wives: Sarai and Milcah, Haran’s daughter. Marriages knit the wounded family together.

Human agency again—taking wives, naming them. The household that will hear God’s call is being formed in ordinary covenanting, including a brother’s child as Nahor’s wife.
verses.reformedNotes:
Abram and Nahor both marry, and the text names both wives. Milcah’s father is the dead Haran; Iscah is mentioned and left.

God is stocking the family that will later supply Rebekah from Nahor’s line. Even the in-laws of Abram sit inside providence.

verses.text: Sarai was barren. She had no child.
verses.arminianNotes:
The promise-line arrives at an empty cradle before any promise is spoken.

The passage carries the ache. God will later give Isaac by gracious power; here the text simply tells the truth. Barrenness is the human condition into which the call must come. Hope will have to be gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
The narrator underlines barrenness twice: barren, no child. Calvin saw God designing to show, in Abram’s person, how the church would arise—as from a dry root.

The line God has so carefully listed ends, humanly, in a closed womb. The next chapter’s offspring-promise will shine against this sentence. Election and miracle will have to do what years and names cannot.

verses.text: Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran, his son’s son, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, his son Abram’s wife. They went from Ur of the Chaldees, to go into the land of Canaan. They came to Haran and lived there.
verses.arminianNotes:
Terah takes Abram, Lot, and Sarai from Ur toward Canaan, then settles in Haran. The aim is Canaan; the halt is Haran. Motive is mixed in the text—a family move later revealed as tied to God’s call.

They go forth together, then stop. Settling short of Canaan is a human pause. Chapter 12 will require Abram to finish what Haran interrupted. Grace already has them on the road; the stop is not the destination.
verses.reformedNotes:
The caravan leaves Ur for Canaan and sits down in Haran. Moses lets Terah’s name lead, yet the destination is the land God will specify.

This is setup, not arrival. Providence extracts the household from Chaldea and holds them in Haran until Terah’s death and Abram’s call. The stop is God’s timing as much as a family’s weariness.
verses.keyContrast: Both see Ur-to-Canaan as the true direction and Haran as a halt. Arminians stress a responsible settling short of the land—movement that must later become Abram’s obedience; Reformed commentators stress that God is relocating the chosen household on His schedule, Haran included.

verses.text: The days of Terah were two hundred five years. Terah died in Haran.
verses.arminianNotes:
Terah’s days are two hundred five years; he dies in Haran. The chapter ends at a graveside on the way, not in Canaan.

A father dies mid-journey, and the son will have to hear a fresh word. Ordinary years, a historical death, and a city that is not the promised land—this is how Genesis prepares chapter 12. The call will not land on a man with no history.
verses.reformedNotes:
Terah dies in Haran. The genealogy’s last number is a death, and the place is still not Canaan.

God has brought the line from Shem to a grave in Mesopotamia so that the next sentence can be, “Go.” The promise-line is intact; the father is buried; the call of chapter 12 will be pure initiative, already prepared by these ordinary years.
